# Surgical and Procedural Treatments

Bariatric surgery represents the most potent and durable intervention currently available for severe obesity, producing sustained weight loss that far exceeds what is achievable through lifestyle modification or pharmacotherapy alone. Over the past three decades, the field has evolved from open procedures with substantial perioperative mortality to laparoscopic and robotic techniques associated with 30-day mortality rates comparable to common elective operations. The mechanistic understanding of bariatric surgery has likewise undergone a conceptual revolution: procedures once characterised purely by mechanical restriction or nutrient malabsorption are now understood to exert profound neuroendocrine, metabolic, and microbiome-mediated effects that operate independently of caloric restriction.

## Types of Bariatric Surgery

The principal bariatric procedures differ substantially in their anatomical modifications, mechanisms of action, magnitude of weight loss, and risk profiles. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) is widely considered the historical gold standard. It creates a small gastric pouch of 15–30 mL that is anastomosed to a Roux limb of jejunum, thereby bypassing the gastric fundus, antrum, duodenum, and proximal 100–150 cm of small bowel. This combined restrictive and malabsorptive anatomy produces 60–80% excess weight loss (EWL) at five years, together with dramatic remission of type 2 diabetes (T2D) and other metabolic comorbidities. The procedure's complexity and the permanence of its intestinal rerouting confer both superior metabolic efficacy and an obligate requirement for lifelong nutritional surveillance.

Sleeve gastrectomy (SG) has displaced RYGB as the most commonly performed bariatric procedure worldwide, now accounting for approximately 60% of all operations. SG is a purely restrictive procedure that removes approximately 80% of the stomach along the greater curvature, leaving a tubular gastric remnant of approximately 60–150 mL. The absence of an intestinal anastomosis simplifies the operation, reduces early complication rates, and preserves duodenal continuity, facilitating endoscopic access to the biliary tree post-operatively. Typical EWL is 50–70% at five years. Although SG lacks the intestinal bypass component of RYGB, post-operative reductions in ghrelin — a primary driver of hunger — and marked increases in GLP-1 and peptide YY (PYY) contribute substantially to appetite suppression and metabolic improvement beyond what restriction alone would predict.

Laparoscopic adjustable gastric band (LAGB) was introduced in the 1990s as a minimally invasive and fully reversible approach. By placing an adjustable silicone band around the gastric cardia, LAGB generates a small proximal pouch that slows gastric emptying. While providing 40–55% EWL in early trials, LAGB has been largely abandoned over the past decade owing to inferior long-term outcomes, band slippage, erosion, and exceptionally high reoperation rates exceeding 50% at ten years. Most centres now reserve the band for patients in whom other procedures carry prohibitive anaesthetic risk.

Biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPD-DS) offers the highest degree of weight loss among standard bariatric operations, with EWL typically exceeding 70–80%. The procedure combines a sleeve gastrectomy with diversion of biliopancreatic secretions to a short common alimentary channel, producing profound malabsorption of macronutrients. This efficacy comes at the cost of the greatest risk of protein malnutrition, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and long-term metabolic complications; BPD-DS is therefore reserved for patients with BMI above 50 kg/m² or those with severe, treatment-refractory metabolic disease. The one-anastomosis gastric bypass (OAGB, or mini-bypass) is a more recently codified alternative that creates a long gastric tube anastomosed to a jejunal loop approximately 200 cm from the ligament of Treitz. Emerging data suggest that OAGB achieves weight loss and T2D remission rates comparable to RYGB with lower operative complexity, and its adoption is growing internationally.

## Long-term Outcomes: The Swedish Obese Subjects Study

The most comprehensive and influential dataset on the long-term effects of bariatric surgery derives from the Swedish Obese Subjects (SOS) study, a prospective, controlled intervention trial that enrolled 4,047 severely obese patients across 25 surgical and 480 primary care centres in Sweden. @Sjoström2004Lifestyle reported the 10-year metabolic outcomes of the SOS cohort, demonstrating that the surgery group maintained a mean weight reduction of 16.1% from baseline at ten years compared with just 1.6% in conventionally treated controls. Over the same period, the cumulative incidence of T2D was reduced by 86% in the surgical group at the eight-year endpoint, a magnitude of prevention unprecedented in any pharmacological or lifestyle trial.

Mortality outcomes from the SOS study were reported by @Sjoström2007Effects in a landmark analysis of 2,010 surgical patients and 2,037 matched controls with a mean follow-up of 10.9 years. Bariatric surgery was associated with an adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause mortality of 0.71 (95% CI 0.54–0.92; p = 0.01), corresponding to a 29% relative reduction in mortality. Deaths from myocardial infarction and cancer were both significantly lower in the surgical cohort. The cardiovascular implications were elaborated further by @Sjoström2012Bariatric, who reported that bariatric surgery reduced the composite endpoint of fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events with a hazard ratio of 0.67 (95% CI 0.54–0.83; p = 0.0002), driven particularly by reductions in fatal myocardial infarction and fatal stroke. These findings established bariatric surgery as an intervention that not only reduces weight but materially alters the natural history of cardiovascular disease in people with severe obesity.

## Bariatric Surgery vs Intensive Medical Therapy for T2D

Several randomised controlled trials have directly compared bariatric surgery with intensive medical therapy for patients with obesity and T2D, consistently demonstrating superiority of the surgical approach for glycaemic control. The STAMPEDE trial [@Schauer2017Bariatric], which enrolled 150 participants with T2D and BMI ranging from 27 to 43 kg/m², provided five-year outcomes of three randomly assigned treatment arms: RYGB, sleeve gastrectomy, and intensive medical therapy. At five years, RYGB produced a mean weight loss of 23.4% from baseline, sleeve gastrectomy 19.0%, and intensive medical therapy 5.4%. The primary endpoint of HbA1c below 6.0% without antidiabetic medications was achieved by 29% of the RYGB group and 23% of the sleeve gastrectomy group, compared with only 5% of the medically treated group. Importantly, this superiority of surgical T2D remission persisted despite modest weight regain in the surgical arms between years two and five, indicating that metabolic benefits are not entirely explained by weight loss.

@Mingrone2012Bariatric reported a complementary Italian RCT of 60 patients with long-standing T2D (mean duration approximately nine years) randomised to RYGB, BPD, or conventional medical therapy. At two years, complete T2D remission — defined as HbA1c below 6.5% with discontinuation of all antidiabetic medications — was achieved in 75% of RYGB patients and 95% of BPD patients, compared with 0% in the conventionally treated group. The rapidity of remission, often occurring within days to weeks of surgery and before substantial weight loss, pointed unambiguously toward weight-independent mechanisms. The Utah Gastric Bypass cohort study [@Adams2007Longterm], which compared 9,949 patients who underwent gastric bypass surgery with 9,628 matched obese controls over a mean follow-up of 7.1 years, demonstrated a 40% reduction in all-cause mortality (18.7 vs 28.2 deaths per 10,000 person-years). The specificity of this survival benefit was especially pronounced for cause-specific mortality: T2D-related deaths were reduced by 92%, and cardiovascular deaths by 59%.

## Mechanisms Beyond Restriction and Malabsorption

The neuroendocrine consequences of bariatric surgery extend far beyond simple caloric restriction or nutrient malabsorption. Following both RYGB and sleeve gastrectomy, dramatic post-prandial increases in GLP-1 and PYY are detectable within days of surgery, well before clinically significant weight loss has occurred [@Batterham2016Neuroendocrine]. These hormonal changes reduce appetite, improve insulin secretion and sensitivity, and contribute directly to T2D remission independently of weight-mediated effects. Emerging evidence also implicates the bile acid–FXR–TGR5 signalling axis, with post-surgical changes in enterohepatic bile acid circulation driving beneficial effects on hepatic glucose metabolism and energy expenditure. Fibroblast growth factors FGF-19 and FGF-21 are likewise altered by intestinal rerouting, further contributing to improved insulin sensitivity and lipid metabolism.

The role of the gut microbiome in mediating post-surgical metabolic benefits has been demonstrated elegantly in germ-free mouse experiments, in which animals colonised with intestinal microbiota from post-RYGB donors gained significantly less weight than those receiving pre-operative microbiota, despite consuming comparable diets. At the neural level, bariatric surgery remodels food reward circuitry, reducing behavioural preference for high-fat and high-sugar foods in a manner consistent with changes observed in mesolimbic dopamine pathways. The landmark meta-analysis of 22,094 patients by @Buchwald2004Bariatric documented the breadth of metabolic improvement achievable through bariatric surgery: T2D resolved in 76.8% of patients, dyslipidaemia improved in 70%, hypertension resolved in 61.7%, and obstructive sleep apnoea resolved in 85.7% — findings that have been replicated and extended in subsequent prospective cohorts.

## Patient Selection and Surgical Criteria

Patient selection criteria for bariatric surgery were first formalised in the 1991 NIH Consensus Statement, which established BMI thresholds of 40 kg/m² or 35 kg/m² with significant comorbidities including T2D, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea, or non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, combined with failure of at least six months of supervised weight management and absence of specific contraindications. These criteria have remained the operational standard in most health systems, though they are increasingly recognised as overly restrictive. Updated ASMBS/IFSO guidance issued in 2022 acknowledges that metabolic surgery should be considered for patients with T2D and BMI as low as 30–35 kg/m², and for patients of Asian ethnicity with BMI above 27.5 kg/m² in the presence of obesity-related comorbidities, reflecting the higher metabolic risk at lower absolute BMI in this population.

Perioperative safety has improved dramatically with the transition to laparoscopic techniques and the concentration of bariatric procedures in high-volume centres. The LABS-1 study [@Flum2009Perioperative], which prospectively enrolled 4,610 patients across ten US clinical centres, reported composite 30-day adverse event rates of 4.3% for RYGB, 2.1% for sleeve gastrectomy, and 1.0% for adjustable gastric banding, with an overall 30-day mortality of 0.3% — comparable to laparoscopic cholecystectomy. These outcomes exhibited a clear volume–outcome relationship, with higher-volume centres achieving significantly lower complication rates. Long-term nutritional management remains a non-negotiable component of post-surgical care; @Mechanick2020Clinical guidelines specify lifelong supplementation with vitamins B12, D, iron, calcium, and folate, with monitoring intervals that intensify whenever weight regain or clinical symptoms suggest nutritional compromise.

## Endoscopic and Minimally Invasive Procedures

Endoscopic bariatric therapies have emerged as a distinct category that occupies the treatment space between pharmacotherapy and surgical intervention. Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) employs suture-based endoscopic plication along the gastric greater curvature to reduce gastric volume without incisions or general anaesthesia. @AbuDayyeh2015Endoscopic demonstrated that ESG alters gastric emptying physiology and achieves approximately 15% total body weight loss at one year, with a safety profile substantially more favourable than surgical sleeve gastrectomy. ESG is currently employed both as a definitive treatment in patients who decline or are not candidates for surgery and as a bridge strategy to reduce operative risk prior to bariatric procedures. Intragastric balloon systems, which temporarily occupy gastric volume to induce early satiety, produce 10–15% weight loss over a six-month treatment period; they are removed endoscopically and represent a short-term, reversible adjunct rather than a standalone long-term intervention. Additional endoluminal approaches — including transpyloric shuttle devices and endoluminal bypass sleeves designed to replicate duodenal exclusion — remain under active investigation in phase 2 and phase 3 clinical trials. The collective advantage of endoscopic therapies is their reversibility, the absence of surgical incisions, and an overall lower procedural risk; their principal limitations are durability, significant operator skill dependence, and a more limited evidence base compared with surgical procedures.
